items.title: Protein Language Model-Conditioned Graph Neural Networks for Multitask Ligand Activity Prediction Across Human GPCRs
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting ligand activity across G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) requires models that capture both molecular structure and receptor-specific information while remaining robust to chemical and target-domain shifts. We developed a multimodal graph neural network that combines explicit ligand molecular graphs with frozen protein language model representations of GPCR sequences and jointly predicts quantitative pActivity and binary activity. The model was trained on 271,739 curated ligand-GPCR pairs spanning 183,694 ligands and 216 human GPCRs and evaluated using random, Bemis-Murcko scaffold, and strict cold-ligand partitions. With ESM-2 650M receptor embeddings, the selected model achieved mean absolute errors of 0.513 {+/-} 0.006, 0.540 {+/-} 0.006, and 0.641 {+/-} 0.005 pActivity units under random, cold-ligand, and scaffold evaluation, respectively, substantially outperforming a protein-aware fixed-feature multilayer perceptron and consistently improving quantitative prediction over a matched GINE reference. Removing receptor embeddings markedly degraded both regression and classification, whereas differences among ESM-2 35M, ESM-2 650M, and ProtT5 were comparatively small. Independent evaluation on 6,319 ChEMBL 37/BindingDB pairs revealed a substantial external domain shift, with mean absolute error increasing to approximately 0.94-0.95 despite chemically stringent internal validation. Nevertheless, receptor-specific information remained highly informative in a DRD2-DRD3 selectivity analysis: the cold-ligand ensemble achieved R^2 = 0.853, Spearman {rho} = 0.916, and ROC-AUC = 0.966 for strong DRD3 selectivity, whereas the receptor-independent ablation approached chance-level discrimination. These results establish protein-language-model-conditioned molecular graph learning as a scalable strategy for GPCR bioactivity prediction while identifying chemotype novelty, external-domain transfer, and richer ligand-receptor interaction representations as key remaining challenges.

items.title: Isotope Effects at Classical Cost through Mass-Differentiable Machine Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Isotope effects govern fractionation and modulate reactivity, with applications from hydrogen energy to environmental science and catalysis, yet predicting them requires resolving small isotope-dependent free-energy differences that remain very challenging for conventional path-integral simulations in complex systems. Here we introduce iso-EPIGS, a path-integral coarse-graining framework built on a mass-differentiable neural network that reconstructs the mass- and temperature-dependent path integral centroid free-energy surface. Classical molecular dynamics on the learned surface yields rigorous isotope-resolved thermodynamics without explicit path-integral sampling. Benchmarks spanning gas, liquid, and crystalline phases, including liquid water and oxalic acid crystal, reproduce reference path-integral isotope free-energy differences, enthalpies, and lattice parameters at near classical computational cost. Crucially, iso-EPIGS trained solely on all-H and all-D isotopologues retains high accuracy for unseen partially deuterated isotopologues, demonstrating robust transferability across nuclear masses. Iso-EPIGS makes accurate isotope-effect simulations feasible for complex systems and lays the groundwork for foundation models of isotope effects across chemical space.

items.title: The Pnictogen Oracle Provider: Multi-Fidelity Graph Landscapes To Benchmark Molecular Optimization
items.abstract_or_text: The informed discovery and inverse design of new molecules and materials is among the most active applications of data-driven procedures, such as statistical learning, to chemical problems. These approaches involve two key aspects: the dataset, and the exploration algorithms. Here, we cover both of these dimensions by introducing POP (Pnictogen Oracle Provider), a platform comprised by an extensive graph database and an optimization toolkit. The database contains almost 200,000 structures for phosphines, amines and arsines at different fidelity levels, explicitly including failed calculations and enforcing a topology based on substituent-level mutation operations. On the other hand, the software toolkit streamlines the application of optimization algorithms (search policies and predictive oracles) to such databases, pushing forward the development of benchmarks. We explore the baseline application of a varied set of such methods—evolutionary algorithms, Bayesian Optimization, LLM-based procedures and multifidelity approaches—to the optimization of a key property: the HOMO-LUMO gap across each of the three ligand families. In this manner, we reveal the relevance of graph topology in the guidance of these algorithms, as well as the performance differences these baseline methods depending on the particularities of each of the ligand families.

items.title: SIMORGH: Ensemble-Aware Geometric Deep Learning for Apo-State and Cryptic Ligand Binding Site Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Most computational methods identify protein-ligand binding sites from ligand-bound (holo) protein structures, where the binding pocket is already preorganized. Although convenient for benchmarking, this setting differs from the practical drug discovery scenario, in which binding sites must be inferred from ligand-free (apo) proteins. In fact, binding-competent conformations may represent only a subset of the accessible structural ensemble, while transient and cryptic pockets can emerge through conformational fluctuations. Consequently, prediction from a single static structure is often insufficient. Here we present SIMORGH, an ensemble-aware SE(3)-equivariant geometric learning framework that predicts ligand binding sites by integrating information across protein conformational ensembles. SIMORGH employs a two-stage architecture consisting of a structure-level equivariant encoder that learns geometric representations from individual conformations and a lightweight ensemble-level aggregation module that combines them into residue-level binding predictions while scaling near-linearly with both protein and ensemble size. We evaluate SIMORGH across multiple complementary settings, including the PLINDER apo benchmark, molecular dynamics trajectories spanning more than 200 cryptic-pocket proteins, and established community benchmarks. SIMORGH consistently outperforms existing static and dynamics-aware methods under the challenging ligand-free setting, while identifying cryptic binding pockets, maintaining strong prediction consistency between paired apo and holo structures, and scaling efficiently to large multi-chain complexes. To facilitate reproducible, transparent, and accessible use, Simorgh is available through the Galaxy Europe server (https://usegalaxy.eu).

items.title: Paper2CIF: An AI Agent for Reconstructing Atomistic Models to Discover Structure-Reactivity Relationships
items.abstract_or_text: Reinterpreting published chemical findings requires explicit atomic structures that connect experimental observations with reactivity. Here we report Paper2CIF, an artificial intelligence (AI) agent that reconstructs sample-specific atomic structures from published chemical evidence for structure-reactivity relationship investigations. Across 171 interdisciplinary articles, Paper2CIF achieves 97.08% phase identification accuracy and 91.23% final structural accuracy, with correct structures satisfying all applicable reported constraints, including composition, site occupancy, and local coordination. Calculations on reconstructed BiVO4 structures reveal distortion-dependent spatial contributions to the transition dipole, guiding targeted synthesis toward enhanced near-edge photon conversion. The resulting BiVO4-based Z-scheme pair exhibits a 3.47-fold increase in apparent quantum yield from 4.51% to 15.64% at 475 nm, compared with a 1.03-fold increase from 18.51% to 19.02% at 365 nm. The solar-to-hydrogen efficiency increases from 0.969% to 1.448% for overall water splitting. Paper2CIF establishes atomic reconstruction as a common basis for deriving chemical mechanisms from published evidence and translating them into experimentally testable principles for materials synthesis.

items.title: Structuring High-Entropy Oxides at the Nanoscale: Ordered Mesoporous (CrMnFeCoNi)Ox Thin Films for High-Performance Oxygen Evolution Reaction Catalysis
items.abstract_or_text: The synthesis of high-entropy oxides (HEOs) with nanoscale architectures is challenging, since both the peculiar crystalline structure with statistical element occupancy and the desired nanomorphology must be controlled. Here, ordered mesoporous (spinel) (CrMnFeCoNi)Ox HEO thin films were prepared via soft-templating and dip-coating under tailored synthesis conditions, and the influence of calcination temperature on their structural evolution and alkaline oxygen evolution reaction (OER) performance was investigated. Electron microscopy revealed a temperature-dependent development of an ordered mesoporous architecture with 15–20 nm pores using polyisobutylene-block-poly(ethylene oxide) (PIB-b-PEO) as structure-directing agent. Energy-dispersive spectroscopy and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy demonstrated a near-equiatomic, spatially homogeneous distribution of all transition metals at the surface and in the bulk. Transmission electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction revealed a temperature-induced transition from an amorphous to nanocrystalline cubic spinel structure at 600 °C. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated a transformation from a high-valence, defective/hydroxylated surface composition rich in Cr6+, Mn3+, Co2+, and Ni2+ species at 300–400 °C to more low-valence surface states with increased lattice-oxygen contribution at 500–600 °C. The mesoporous HEO thin film annealed at 400 °C for 5 min exhibited one of the best OER performances ever reported (η10 = 273 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and Rct = 3.9 Ω at 1.5 V vs. RHE) in alkaline electrolyte. Overall, the structural evolution and OER performance of HEO thin films follow a temperature-dependent activity trend based on the balance and interplay of surface area, crystallinity, oxygen defects, and catalytically active species at the surface, highlighting the necessity of precise control of the synthesis conditions and formulation of structure-property relationships for improving the OER performance of compositionally complex catalysts.

items.title: YB_Mol Studio: an agent-integrated visual editing platform for molecular and materials design
items.abstract_or_text: Molecular and materials design requires researchers to inspect structures, edit molecular objects and connect each change to computation. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents add another operating mode: they need executable molecular operations, visible intermediate states and a way to continue from prior results. Here we present YB_Mol Studio, an agent-integrated visual editing platform for molecular and materials design. Its molecular design core, yb_mol, represents atoms, bonds, coordinates, structural hierarchy and periodic information in editable molecular objects. Studio connects this core to direct visual editing, YB_Agent execution, a persistent Live workspace and local or remote scientific computation. Researchers can select and modify structures through the interface, inspect resulting states and continue a design manually or with the agent. YB_Agent can execute molecular operations through yb_mol, use specialist prediction or evaluation methods and publish results back into the same workspace. Molecular-object comparisons and operation benchmarks characterize the platform foundation, while three application workspaces exercise it on biomolecular and periodic-material workloads. YB_Mol Studio links human judgment, interactive visualization, agent execution and computational feedback in one continuing design environment.

items.title: Large-Scale Benchmarking of Quantum Neural Network Configurations for Financial Time Series Forecasting
items.abstract_or_text: Quantum machine learning, and quantum neural networks (QNNs) in particular, are advancing fields with growing potential. Although systematic comparisons of QNN configurations have been explored primarily for classification tasks, comparatively little attention has been given to regression problems, particularly financial time series forecasting. This study presents a large-scale systematic comparative evaluation of QNN component configurations for financial time series forecasting, using the GBP/USD spot exchange rate as a case study. A grid search across encoding methods, ansatz designs, qubit counts, layer depths, and cost functions yields 1,368 distinct model configurations, each evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, computational cost, and convergence behaviour. The results reveal unique insights into how the choice of methods influences performance, such as that gate selection and arrangement are more critical to model success than raw parameter count, and that entanglement is a system-level property of the full circuit rather than solely at the ansatz level. The best-performing QNN configuration achieves an R^2 score of 0.985, outperforming a classical BiLSTM baseline. Additionally, the impact of real quantum hardware noise is assessed through execution on the IQM Emerald device, revealing that gate errors and decoherence represent a significant barrier to practical deployment, with gate selection and circuit depth identified as key determinants of hardware noise resilience. Overall, the findings provide practical architectural guidance for QNN design and establish a baseline characterisation of QNN noise sensitivity on near-term quantum devices.

items.title: Structure Tax: How Structured Output affects LLMs Performance
items.abstract_or_text: Deploying large language models in production often requires constraining outputs to structured formats such as JSON or XML, and prior work treats the resulting accuracy loss as an inherent `structure tax'. We re-examine this claim by evaluating a battery of models, datasets and schemas, measuring task accuracy, confidence calibration, and hidden-state geometry. The tax turns out to depend on schema design rather than on structure per se: reasoning-first field ordering matches or exceeds free-form accuracy, while answer-first ordering causes steep drops, particularly in smaller models. Format sensitivity scales inversely with a task's own structural constraints, and schemas that preserve reasoning order also improve calibration with CKA showing greater separability between correct and incorrect representations in middle transformer layers. Our findings indicate that properly designed structured formats can match or exceed free-form performance, reframing the critical question from `whether to structure' to `how to structure' for optimal reasoning preservation.

items.title: Beyond Imitation: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Peer Review
items.abstract_or_text: The rapid growth of scientific publishing has strained peer review, particularly in machine learning, raising concerns about declining review quality and increasing reviewer workload. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as automated review assistants, yet their evaluation has focused largely on imitating human-written reviews rather than supporting the core functions of peer review. Here, we introduce a verification-centric perspective on LLM-assisted peer review, emphasizing error detection as a critical and resource-intensive task. We present a scalable benchmark that evaluates review systems' ability to identify logical contradictions, constructed through synthetic insertion of errors into conference papers, yielding unambiguous evaluation targets and enabling systematic comparison. We further propose a Multi-Layered Review (MLR) framework that prioritizes detailed manuscript comprehension before review generation, aligning more closely with human reviewing practices while improving token efficiency. Across evaluations, our approach demonstrates strong alignment with human review scores, achieves high error detection performance, and provides complementary perspectives on reviewer focus. These improvements can be attributed to both the choice of the underlying LLM and the design of our system. At the same time, we corroborate persistent vulnerabilities to adversarial manipulation, underscoring the need for robustness in automated review systems. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous, error-focused evaluation to guide responsible deployment of LLM-based tools in peer review and other critical scientific workflows.

items.title: Non-equilibrium modeling of flux through biomolecular condensates
items.abstract_or_text: Cellular biomolecular condensates function far from equilibrium, sustained by continuous influx and efflux of molecular components. Notable examples include the nucleolus, P-bodies, and stress granules, in which regulated molecular transport is essential for their function. Experimental characterization of molecular flux through condensates remains challenging due to limitations in spatiotemporal resolution, making computational approaches a powerful alternative for systematic investigation. Here, we present a computational approach (TRACE) to model molecular transport through biomolecular condensates under non-equilibrium steady-state conditions at residue-level resolution. Using TRACE, we systematically probe physicochemical factors that govern molecular flux through model condensates. We find that protein sequence composition and patterning determine the internal `mesh size' of the condensates, which strongly dictates molecular transport efficiency, and the ballistic-to-diffusive dynamics crossover of the fluxing molecules. We also find that molecule stiffness can enhance their flux by exposing larger surface for intermolecular interactions. Furthermore, we find that modulating host-guest interactions can modulate solubility and friction which jointly governs molecular flux. Finally, we use our framework to show that crosslinking reduces condensate pore size, hindering molecular flux -- consistent with experimental observations of dextran diffusion through nucleolar phases. Collectively, these insights provide a basis for rationally tuning condensate-mediated molecular flux, with potential applications in therapeutics and soft material design.

items.title: Beyond Distributional Fidelity: Causal-Penalized Diffusion for Synthetic Tabular Data
items.abstract_or_text: Synthetic tabular generators are commonly optimized for distributional fidelity, but statistical similarity alone does not guarantee preservation of causal effects. In this paper, we study whether causal fidelity can be improved directly within a fully generative tabular model. Causal Fidelity is defined with respect to a target estimand as the discrepancy between inferential distributions obtained from real and synthetic data, and theoretical results show that high statistical fidelity does not generally imply high causal fidelity. We then propose a causal-fidelity-aware training framework which adds a causal discrepancy penalty to the generative objective. The framework is instantiated with a causal-penalized TabDDPM and optimized using an on-policy score-function estimator. We further establish conditions under which causal regularization improves expected causal fidelity. Experiments across diverse treatment-effect simulations and two benchmark datasets evaluate the ability of our method to improve causal fidelity while preserving competitive statistical fidelity.

items.title: PRMT5 inhibition induces a histone methylation switch that drives chromatin plasticity, drug resistance, and metastatic progression
items.abstract_or_text: PRMT5 is the major type II protein arginine methyltransferase, regulating fundamental processes including transcription, splicing, and translation. Its expression is restricted to stem and progenitor cells but reactivated in many tumors. Numerous PRMT5 inhibitors (PRMT5i) have been developed, and several are currently in clinical trials. Their efficacy is largely attributed to disruption of PRMT5's role in splicing. Here we show that PRMT5i produce dichotomous effects in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD): they induce lethal splicing defects but also trigger epigenetic changes that actively enable acquisition of drug resistance. Of concern, the resulting stably resistant populations have undergone accelerated dedifferentiation, gaining molecular and phenotypic hallmarks of metastatic disease. Moreover, even brief PRMT5i treatment of drug-naive tumors is sufficient to drive disease progression in vivo. This epigenetic rewiring reflects a previously unappreciated dominance of PRMT5 over PRMT1, arising from differential subcellular localization. Our data indicate that cytoplasmic PRMT5 likely dimethylates histones symmetrically before nuclear import. PRMT5i block this, allowing unmodified histones to reach nuclear PRMT1 and undergo asymmetric dimethylation instead. This symmetric-to-asymmetric switch flips histones from repressive to activating states, yielding rapid chromatin opening and derepression of lineage programs, a subset of which are selected for and retained in resistant cells. Accordingly, inhibition of asymmetric dimethylation suppresses PRMT5i-induced chromatin derepression and synergizes strongly with PRMT5 inhibition. Finally, endogenous PRMT5 suppression in MTAP-deficient human cells partially engages this switch, and CDKN2A/MTAP-deficient tumors are correspondingly more dedifferentiated. Thus, PRMT5i create a splicing vulnerability while simultaneously licensing epigenetic escape toward a more dedifferentiated and aggressive cell state.

items.title: QMzyme: A Python Package for Automated and Systematic QM-based Enzyme Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce QMzyme, a Python package to automate the generation of Quantum mechanics (QM)-based enzyme models. QM calculations on enzymes are computationally challenging because full enzyme systems typically contain thousands of atoms, placing accurate QM treatments beyond practical computational limits.Therefore, QM-based enzyme studies rely on identifying a subset of atoms that captures the essential chemistry of the reaction environment, enabling tractable yet chemically meaningful calculations. However, constructing these reduced models requires numerous user-defined decisions, including selection of the starting structure, identification of atoms to include in the QM region, and definition of truncation strategies for QM-only models, all of which can substantially influence the resulting calculations. QMzyme aims to provide the community with a flexible and extensible framework for automated, systematic generation of QM-based enzyme models, enabling researchers to more rigorously evaluate how model construction decisions influence computational outcomes while improving reproducibility and transparency across workflows. By facilitating high-throughput generation and analysis of QM enzyme models, QMzyme supports largescale, data-driven investigations of enzyme structure, function, and reactivity. This effort is especially crucial for the creation of large, chemically consistent datasets that can support emergent artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches for accelerated digital discovery in enzymology and biocatalysis.

items.title: TRACE: Diagnosing Verifier Brittleness in Agentic Evaluation
items.abstract_or_text: Verifier scores now serve as both benchmark metrics and training rewards for large language model (LLM) agents, and a change in score is routinely read as a change in capability. It may instead reflect a change in the evaluation. We introduce TRACE, a protocol that turns a score change from a verdict into a testable diagnosis: it applies a targeted change to one part of an evaluation, compares paired runs, checks whether the agent's behavior changed, and rescores unchanged trajectories to test whether the scoring rule is responsible. In a controlled suite of 25 synthetic tasks, renaming tools lowers a scripted agent's score by 0.250 even though it performs exactly the same operations; restoring the original names at scoring time closes the entire gap, while the same mutation exposes a genuine behavioral failure in a second agent. On public τ^2-bench tasks with four LLM agents, an initial 30-task study finds mixed reward changes whose one clear effect does not replicate. In a larger follow-up on 88 new tasks with repeated runs per condition, renaming tools or reformatting tool outputs leaves reward unchanged to within \pm0.10 for seven of eight agent-change pairs, whereas tool names that deliberately mislead lower every agent's reward by 0.20-0.44, showing that the setup can detect real effects. Identical reruns flip 15-36% of task outcomes, so single-run comparisons cannot separate presentation effects from run-to-run variation. Two frontier LLM judges give consistent verdicts when a fixed trajectory is presented differently, yet disagree with each other on 57% of the same records, largely because one grades procedure rather than outcome. TRACE thus separates what a score change says about the agent from what it says about the measurement.

items.title: Adapting English Quality Classifiers for Multilingual LLM Pretraining Data Selection
items.abstract_or_text: Recent advances in large language model (LLM) pretraining highlight the role of high-quality training data in improving performance. While model-based filtering has proven effective in selecting high-quality subsets from web-scale corpora, especially for high-resource languages, low-resource languages face challenges due to limited availability of annotated data. This work explores extending quality filtering to over 100 languages by proposing a multilingual adaptation approach that converts an existing English quality classifier into a multilingual variant. Our approach proposes training a small multi-layer perceptron on top of Transformer encoder-only model embeddings, using multilingual text as input and scores obtained from English classifiers applied to machine-translated text as labels. Our 1B, 3B and 8B scale experiments show that our approach maintains the downstream LLM benchmark performance of existing multilingual model-based filtering baselines, without harming regional and cultural knowledge benchmarks. To further evaluate cross-lingual generalization, we compare classifier scores of high-quality synthetic data and web samples, and the correlation of classifier scores with LLM-based ones, revealing that the classifier can learn the scoring criteria of its original English variant, even for languages not included in its training data.

items.title: Closed-loop evaluation of LLM agents for embedded software development
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as coding agents that edit files, run builds and tests, inspect execution results, and repair software iteratively. Embedded firmware is a demanding target because correctness depends on closed-loop behavior under sensing, timing, and safety constraints, not only on static source quality. Yet embedded-agent evaluation remains limited and often emphasizes one-shot synthesis or offline correctness. We present a benchmark for closed-loop evaluation of embedded coding agents. Each task provides a plain-text engineering description, constrained workspace, and visible build-and-runtime surface. The agent must translate requirements into implementation and self-verification steps, then iterate until the required device behavior is achieved. The suite contains five embedded-control tasks and four feedback scenarios: one-shot generation, realistic self-verification, CI-style red/green feedback, and oracle-style detailed feedback. The implementation targets simulated ESP32 firmware for reproducibility. We evaluate seven GPT-family and Qwen-family configurations across five tasks and four scenarios, with three repetitions per condition for 420 runs. gpt-5.4 has the highest pass rate among evaluated configurations but does not saturate the benchmark; qwen3.5-27B is the strongest observed local model; and smaller local models degrade sharply in pass rate and search efficiency. These results suggest that capable local embedded coding agents are emerging.

items.title: Evaluation of synthetic data generation for longitudinal 6-year follow-up subclinical cardiovascular disease data using GAN models
items.abstract_or_text: Although largely preventable, cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. Synthetic data generation (SDG) of health data can facilitate data sharing for research and development of personalised cardiovascular disease prevention tools. Current state-of-the-art SDG methods are limited to cross-sectional data or focused on short-term or in-patient EHR applications lacking benchmarks for generalisability. Since prevention is a long-term longitudinal objective, these limitations must be addressed. We evaluated two tabular generative adversarial networks, TGAN and CTGAN, for privacy and fidelity on a structured 6-year longitudinal trial dataset within CVD prevention. We compared performance with a rudimentary perturbation method. In addition, we performed a variable-wise evaluation and an age-stratified analysis of the higher performing model to assess preservation of clinically relevant characteristics. Overall, CTGAN showed better fidelity than TGAN. The models performed similarly within privacy, showing better results than the perturbation method. CTGAN had lower performance in comparison to the perturbation method within numerical fidelity of continuous variables and overall temporal fidelity. Furthermore, CTGAN's performance was lower for younger age groups than older. CTGAN shows better than or equal performance within fidelity and privacy than TGAN and the perturbation method on a long-term longitudinal dataset within CVD prevention. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study evaluating CTGAN on a longitudinal dataset and our findings suggest that handling of temporal characteristics and imbalanced subgroups need further refinement.

items.title: A deep learning-generated hASIC1a miniprotein inhibitor confers neuroprotection in stroke
items.abstract_or_text: Ion channels remain notoriously recalcitrant drug targets despite their extensive pathophysiological significance. Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that cause neuronal death when excessively activated, such as during ischaemic stroke. This acidosis-driven injury pathway remains unchallenged by existing therapeutics. Here we generate two de novo designed hASIC1a-specific miniproteins by developing a platform that integrates computational miniprotein design, high-throughput automated patch clamp screening, biophysical and structural characterisation, and in vivo validation. We identify a subtype-selective hASIC1a inhibitor, Denasin1, which achieves near-complete inhibition with nanomolar potency. Denasin1 is disordered in solution but adopts the computationally predicted helix-turn-helix fold when bound to the extracellular acidic pocket of hASIC1a. Crucially, Denasin1 reduces infarct volume by > 50% in a murine model of ischaemic stroke. We thereby establish our de novo design platform as a route to develop potent and selective ion channel modulators.

items.title: The Batten disease gene product CLN6 is a glycerophosphoglycerol epimerase that establishes S,S-BMP stereochemistry
items.abstract_or_text: Bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP), a lysosomal phospholipid essential for lipid catabolism and cholesterol clearance, has a noncanonical S,S glycerol configuration found in no other mammalian phospholipid, a feature necessary for its stability in the lysosome. How cells invert glycerol stereochemistry to build S,S-BMP has remained unexplained since this configuration was discovered five decades ago. Here, we show that the endoplasmic reticulum-resident Batten disease protein CLN6 is a Ca2+-dependent epimerase that isomerizes glycerophosphoglycerol (GPG) from R,S-GPG to S,S-GPG. CLN6-deficient cells, mouse tissues, and patient samples predominantly contain R,S-GPG, S,R-lysophosphatidylglycerol (LPG), and R,S-BMP instead of their S,S counterparts, with a net depletion of BMP. Purified CLN6 catalyzes GPG epimerization in vitro, an activity abolished by a pathogenic substitution in its substrate-binding pocket. Consistently, exogenous S,S-GPG restores BMP synthesis and relieves lipid storage in CLN6-null cells. Our work establishes stereochemical commitment upstream of acylation, placing CLN6, CLN8, and CLN5 in sequence in BMP biosynthesis and unifying the lipid defect across these neurodegenerative disorders.

items.title: SCKAnalyzer: A Web Tool for Single-Cycle Kinetics Analysis and Simulation
items.abstract_or_text: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and biolayer interferometry (BLI) are well-established label-free analytical technologies used to determine biomolecular interaction rates (ka, kd) and equilibrium constants (KD). While assays historically rely on multi-cycle kinetics (MCK), this approach requires intermediate surface regeneration, risking sensor degradation and increasing reagent consumption. Single-cycle kinetics (SCK) avoids regeneration by sequentially injecting increasing analyte concentrations. However, implementing SCK workflows on biosensor platforms like the OctetRR8 BLI instrument (Sartorius) remains a challenge due to the lack of built-in or online data analysis tools. To address this, we introduce SCKAnalyzer, a free, user-friendly web application designed for processing and fitting SCK datasets. SCKAnalyzer accepts column-based text files and native raw BLI data (.frd format) from Sartorius instruments, performing data pre-processing and non-linear fitting to a 1:1 interaction model. Additionally, it offers advanced simulation capabilities that allow variable association and dissociation durations across sequential injection steps, a feature absent in existing platforms such as BiacoreTMSimul8. The performance of SCKAnalyzer was experimentally validated using a 3-step SCK method (SCK3) for DNA/RNA duplex formation on a Biacore T200, as well as 4-step (SCK4) and 5-step (SCK5) methods for DNA/DNA duplex formation on an OctetRR8 BLI instrument. Binding parameters (ka, kd, KD) derived from SCKAnalyzer showed excellent agreement with values from established proprietary softwares such as Biacore T200 Evaluation Software v3.2.1 and BIAevaluation v4.1.1. SCKAnalyzer provides a practical alternative to MCK, reducing probe consumption and extending SCK utility across biosensor platforms. SCKAnalyzer is available at sck.iecb.u-bordeaux.fr (source code: github.com/synthaze/sckanalyzer).

items.title: CLN6 is a glycerophosphoglycerol epimerase in bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate biosynthesis
items.abstract_or_text: Lysosomal catabolism depends on bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP), a phospholipid with atypical S,S stereochemistry of unknown biosynthetic origin. CLN8 and CLN5 catalyze sequential acylation steps in BMP synthesis, and their loss of function causes Batten disease, a group of inherited neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders. Here we identify CLN6, a biochemically uncharacterized endoplasmic reticulum protein whose loss also causes Batten disease, as the calcium-dependent glycerophosphoglycerol epimerase that establishes BMP stereochemistry upstream of CLN8. CLN6 deficiency depletes BMP in cells, mice, and patient lysosomes, and reduces lysosomal hydrolase levels. BMP-precursor supplementation bypasses CLN6, restores BMP and increases hydrolase abundance in CLN6-deficient cells and mice. These findings place three Batten disease proteins in a single biosynthetic pathway and reveal BMP deficiency as a reversible cause of disrupted lysosomal hydrolase homeostasis.

items.title: Structured biological evidence enables general-purpose language models to predict bacteriophage-host interactions
items.abstract_or_text: Biological interaction inference often requires integrating heterogeneous evidence that differs in biological meaning, provenance, specificity, and reliability. Existing computational approaches typically compress such evidence into numerical features, aggregate scores, or latent representations before prediction, obscuring the contribution of individual evidence records and limiting interpretation when evidence is conflicting or incomplete. Phage-host interaction prediction provides a demanding test case for this problem, requiring the integration of genomic, functional, and reference-derived evidence with differing coverage, specificity, and reliability. Here we introduce a structured-evidence inference paradigm that retains heterogeneous biological observations as modular, named, and experimentally perturbable records rather than compressing them before prediction. We implement this paradigm in PHI-Reason, which constructs structured textual profiles from genomic annotations, receptor-binding protein homology, nucleotide-neighbour relationships, alignment-free genomic similarity, and available CRISPR spacer information. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) performs inference directly over these structured profiles without task-specific training or manually engineered evidence-fusion rules. Across phage-host benchmarks, PHI-Reason achieved species-level top-1 accuracies of 67.4% and 57.2% on RefSeq-634 and VHDB-3150, respectively, and a multi-host accuracy of 0.673 on the Hi-C cohort, outperforming established numerical methods. On 207 experimentally supported associations from 2025-2026 excluded from the reference corpus, it achieved 52.2% species-level and 90.8% genus-level top-1 accuracy. Evidence perturbations identified nucleotide-neighbour context as the dominant signal and quantified complementary or misleading evidence contributions. Target-conditioned local Jacobian and output-grounding analyses further characterized evidence-dependent inference and departures of generated rationales from the supplied evidence. Extending the framework to eukaryotic virus-host prediction preserved high predictive accuracy (67.0%), supporting cross-domain portability. Moreover, replacing the reasoning LLM with Jev, a typed-decision model, maintained broadly comparable performance across phage-host benchmarks while reducing mean per-query inference time by 11- to 40-fold, supporting the separation of evidence representation from downstream inference. These results establish structured biological evidence as a portable interface between heterogeneous biological observations and downstream inference. By separating evidence representation from the inference engine, this paradigm supports both language-model predictions with inspectable rationales and faster typed decisions for high-throughput prediction, while making the contribution and limits of evidential support directly testable.

items.title: Alkyl-BODIPYs as a Self-Photoredox Catalyst for their Oxidative Hydroxymethylation
items.abstract_or_text: The adoption of photocatalytic approaches for utilising small organic molecules in self‑catalysed reactions offers opportunities in green organic synthesis. We report that alkylated boron‑dipyrromethenes (BODIPYs) act as self‑photoredox catalysts for their own oxidation under mild visible‑light conditions. Using an imidazolinium salt (NHC-H) as a quencher, alkylated BODIPYs are oxidised cleanly to the corresponding hydroxymethyl derivatives in a one‑pot process. Luminescence studies, including Stern–Volmer analysis, support a reductive‑quenching pathway in which the NHC-H transfers an electron to photoexcited BODIPY to give a BODIPY radical anion. The method proceeds without external photocatalysts or stoichiometric oxidants and shows good functional‑group tolerance, highlighting the potential of these chromophores both as substrates and catalytic light absorbers. Moreover, the synthesized molecules were demonstrated to behave as effective passivating agents for layered Mn2+

items.title: Just Weather Scoring: Efficient End-to-end Nowcasting with Distributional Diffusion
items.abstract_or_text: Generative diffusion models are well-suited for probabilistic precipitation nowcasting, but existing approaches often rely on separately trained compression or deterministic forecasting components and remain costly at inference due to iterative denoising. We introduce Just Weather Scoring (JWS), a single-stage, end-to-end diffusion model which addresses both issues by forecasting directly in radar space and enabling few-step generation. Radar-space modeling greatly simplifies training and inference and eliminates uncertainty arising from lossy compression. JWS combines Masked Asynchronous Diffusion, a timestep-sampling scheme that preserves clean context while adapting diffusion training to high-dimensional spatio-temporal data, with a simple scoring-rule objective that aligns training with probabilistic forecasting and unlocks few-step generation. On the SEVIR and MeteoNet benchmarks, JWS achieves state-of-the-art probabilistic forecasting performance at reduced training and inference cost. Even our smallest model remains competitive using substantially fewer parameters and more than 17x faster inference.

items.title: Molecular mechanisms regulating PDE11A4 age-related liquid-liquid phase separation and its reversal by selective PDE11A4-targeted small molecules in cells and brain
items.abstract_or_text: Age-related increases in hippocampal PDE11A expression occur in humans and rodents, causing age-related cognitive decline of social memories. Interestingly, this age-related increase triggers PDE11A4 liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), causing the enzyme to condensate in neurons forming filamentous structures termed "ghost axons". Here we sought to identify molecular mechanisms regulating PDE11A4 LLPS and its reversal by therapeutic agents. PDE11A4 LLPS was increased by broad kinase inhibition and overactivation of the trans-Golgi network (via TGN38 or RhoB) but suppressed by PDE11A4-pS163, PDE11A4-pS239 or a D355A mutation affecting allosteric cGMP-GAF-A interactions. PDE11Ai inhibitors across three scaffolds rapidly reversed PDE11A LLPS independently of their catalytic effects, pS163 or pS239, but rather--at least in part--by reducing PDE11 homodimerization at the GAF-B domain. PDE11Ais blocked exacerbated LLPS caused by age-related PDE11A4 phosphorylation, kinase disruption, and altered proteostasis in hippocampal HT22 neuronal cells. Further, in hippocampus and amygdala of old mice, oral SMQ-03-20 reversed age-related increases in PDE11A4 condensation in ghost axons and protein expression of immunoglobulin light chains (a marker of increased blood-brain permeability), with direct correlation between the two measures. These findings suggest PDE11A4 LLPS is a regulated and druggable mechanism contributing to age-related hippocampal pathology.\

items.title: Machine learning classifies subcellular Golgi morphology from imaging flow cytometry during inflammatory activation: an exploratory study
items.abstract_or_text: Inflammatory activation remodels the Golgi apparatus to meet increased secretory demand, yet whether these structural changes carry computationally accessible information about immune cell state has not been explored. Here we show that machine learning applied to imaging flow cytometry images of the Golgi can distinguish lipopolysaccharide (LPS) treated from control cells. We trained models on Golgi images from human THP-1 monocytes before and 16 h after LPS stimulation in vitro, and from circulating myeloid cells of mice 24 h after intratracheal LPS or saline in vivo. In each dataset, the best-performing model was a deep learning model trained directly on images rather than a classifier using predefined morphometric features. Cross-domain performance varied with the model, transfer direction and use of labelled target data: several deep learning models trained on mouse images classified THP-1 cells above chance without changing model parameters. Grad-CAM highlighted regions within or adjacent to the GM130 fluorescence pattern. These findings indicate that GM130 images carry information associated with LPS treatment that supports classification within and across the two datasets. To our knowledge, this is the first application of supervised deep learning to imaging flow cytometry images of a subcellular organelle for inflammatory phenotyping, establishing organelle level image analysis as a potential complement to molecular assays for immune cell classification.

items.title: Solid-state NMR and first-principle calculations reveal the structure and dynamics of Li-N-H materials
items.abstract_or_text: Lithium-nitrogen-hydrogen (Li-N-H) materials are promising for hydrogen storage, solid-state batteries, and lithium-mediated ammonia synthesis, yet their local structures and proton dynamics remain poorly understood because of compositional disorder and limited sensitivity of conventional diffraction methods. Here, we combine multinuclear solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H, 7Li, 14N, and 15N ssNMR) with first-principles calculations to resolve the atomic environments and dynamics of Li3N, LiNH2, and Li1+xNH2-x (. 7Li NMR and density functional theory calculations identify distinct lithium sites in coexisting α- and β-Li3N phases and in tetragonal LiNH2. 1H and 15N NMR, together with 1H-detected 14N spectroscopy, reveal two distinct domains in synthesized lithium-rich Li1+xNH2-x that are not resolved by laboratory X-ray diffraction. Comparison with calculated NMR parameters assigns these domains to LiNH2 and Li2NH, respectively. Variable-temperature 1H-1H exchange spectroscopy shows that correlations between the two domains arise predominantly from spin diffusion rather than interdomain proton exchange, indicating nanoscale structural heterogeneity within a solid solution. Local proton motion occurs within the Li2NH environment and is restricted in the LiNH­2 domains. These results establish a molecular-level relationship between local structure and proton mobility in Li-N-H materials, providing insights relevant to hydrogen storage, solid-state batteries, and ammonia synthesis.

items.title: New approach for deciphering polyethylene terephthalate (PET)-based plastics’ diols: Application on PET daily-life packaging objects paving their chemical modifications
items.abstract_or_text: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a thermoplastic polyester synthetized from a terephthalic diacid and a diol which is generally ethylene glycol. Given PET prominence in food packaging industry, a detailed study of this polymer is of utmost importance. The identification of the initial diols constituting PET-based bottles and containers along with their structural modifications, due to recycling procedures and/or weathering, is still a challenging research subject. In this study, PET diols were derivatized using a new approach combining an innovative methanolysis-benzoylation methodology with analysis by Orbitrap MS. First, a transesterification with methanol for freeing diols and/or polyols was performed followed by a derivatization with 4-dimethylaminobenzoyl chloride (DMABC) used as benzoylation agent under specific conditions. After reaction post-treatment, the derivatized products were analyzed using ESI ionization on an Orbitrap MS hyphenated to liquid chromatography LC−MS. This method was applied to PET-based daily-life bottles and containers in comparison to authentic diols and copolyesters used as references, showing extra new data on their diols’ composition that may be affected by recycling, manufacturing procedures and/or natural weathering. These PET-based packaging objects were differentiated according to the detected diols along with their oxidized compounds and hydroxy acids. Other polyesters and copolyesters can be studied using this same new strategy.

items.title: Anneal-MaxCal: kinetic ensembles from a Markov model learned along a solute-tempering ladder
items.abstract_or_text: A full characterisation of a molecular system requires its metastable states, their populations and their interconversion rates. Molecular Dynamics can in principle provide this characterisation but is limited by sampling and by force-field inaccuracies. Enhanced sampling addresses the first problem, but typically requires prior knowledge of reaction coordinates or metastable states and often sacrifices the kinetics, while maximum-caliber reweighting by Brotzakis, Vendruscolo and Bolhuis [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A., 118(2):e2012423118, 2021] has been implemented to that matter on reweighting continuous pathways by imposing rate constants as kinetic constraints in two-state protein folding. Here, we introduce Anneal-MaxCal, which tackles both problems by imposing rate constants or time-resolved data on a Markov model learned along an annealed solute-tempering ladder spanning softer to physical interactions. MBAR assigns physical free energies to all 160 cells of a slow TICA subspace, against 79 visited at the physical coupling. The square-root approximation (SqRA), a discretised diffusion on this free-energy landscape, converts these populations into a detailed-balance rate matrix. Its prefactors, which act as a position-dependent diffusivity across each cell face, are learned from transitions at the softer couplings and extrapolated log-linearly to the physical coupling. This yields rates and a committor across the TICA space, although the physical rung contains a single barrier crossing. For alanine dipeptide, 665 ns of simulation give a relaxation time of 5430 {+/-} 996 ps against 4413 {+/-} 446 ps from 15.4 s of unbiased dynamics, whereas a constant prefactor is 2.5 times too slow. Maximum caliber then minimally perturbs this prior, with the posterior populations following from a generalised Doob transform. A synthetic time-resolved density with a tenfold slower back-transition lowers {Delta}F from 5.191 to 2.885 kBT , raises the product-basin population from 0.0055 to 0.0529 and slows relaxation 9.47-fold, leaving the reactant basin unchanged. Forward and backward rates accelerated 3 and 20-fold raise {Delta}F by 1.892 kBT and shorten relaxation from 4818 to 289 ps.

items.title: Memory-Augmented Generative Design of Octahedral Co(II) Complexes with Targeted Zero-Field Splitting
items.abstract_or_text: The discovery of coordination complexes with targeted magnetic anisotropy remains challenging because the enormous chemical space of ligands and coordination environments makes propertydirected molecular design difficult to achieve by conventional screening. Here, we introduce a memoryaugmented generative framework for the inverse design of octahedral Co(II) complexes with targeted zero-field splitting (ZFS). A chemically curated dataset of ~6000 Co(II) complexes, was used to establish a broad electronic-structure landscape spanning positive and negative ZFS regimes. Building on this chemical space, a generative strategy was developed in which ligand structures are iteratively mutated, recombined, and selected according to their predicted magnetic properties, while an elitememory mechanism preserves high-performing molecular motifs and guides subsequent generations toward increasingly favorable candidates. This enables targeted exploration of ligand combinations and coordination environments associated with large negative ZFS while simultaneously controlling rhombicity. The generated complexes were subjected to independent CASSCF calculations, including spin–orbit coupling, to directly validate their magnetic properties. Notably, the generative framework identified candidates with strongly enhanced axial anisotropy, including a representative complex exhibiting D ≈ −223 cm-1 after ab initio validation. The validated candidates reproduced the targeted ZFS with deviations of approximately 15–18 cm-1. These results establish a generative, memory-guided route from ligand design to electronically validated magnetic complexes, providing a practical strategy for discovering previously unexplored Co(II) molecular magnets and advancing molecular-magnet design from screening toward property-directed generation.

items.title: MemTrial: Learning When to Trust Memory in LLM Portfolio Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model (LLM) agents for portfolio management learn from experience: they credit each experience in their memory with the outcome of the decisions that used it. In financial markets, however, this outcome mostly reflects the market move shared by all decisions on that date, so the credit tracks the market rather than the experience, and these agents often do worse than simply holding the equal-weight (1/N) portfolio. We ask how an agent can credit an experience with what it changes, and answer it by putting memory on trial: drafts of the same decision with and without an experience face the same market, so the outcome they share cancels in their difference. Our agent, MemTrial, drafts each decision with eight combinations of its retrieved experiences, chosen by a fractional factorial design, and credits each experience with its Banzhaf value, the average of these differences. As each date occurs once and each draft is a noisy LLM sample, these credits are noisy and may not hold on new dates. MemTrial therefore pools them across dates and similar experiences with a hierarchical Bayesian model, acts on them only after they have predicted unseen dates, and otherwise stays anchored at a conservative reference such as 1/N. On four benchmarks, MemTrial not only benefits from experiences that matter (the best of 15 methods on a semi-synthetic benchmark with known experience quality) but also limits its losses when its values do not hold (at most 2.2\% below 1/N on PortBench and InvestorBench, against 15--38\% for the best experience-learning agent). Averaged over five settings, it improves the utility of the best experience-learning agent by 21.2\%, and with eight LLMs it beats every LLM-based baseline on InvestorBench.

items.title: From Retrieval to Reconstruction: Constructing Evolvable Cognitive Memory for Long-Term Dialogue
items.abstract_or_text: Large Language Models (LLMs) serving as long-term dialogue agents require memory systems that support reliable reasoning over extended interactions. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks typically treat memory as passive storage, making it difficult to distinguish source-attributed beliefs from unattributed event/fact records and to connect evidence dispersed across sessions. We introduce CogMem, a cognitive memory architecture based on the PEC^2F (Person-Event-Concept-Claim-Fact) graph schema. Dedicated Claim nodes preserve the source and target of subjective statements, while Fact and Event nodes represent semantic and episodic knowledge. Dialogue turns are incrementally converted into provenance-aware graph records, consolidated into higher-level facts, and reconciled into temporally scoped Claim views when the same source provides conflicting updates. For retrieval, a rule-based controller driven by LLM intent parsing composes four deterministic graph operators---anchoring, traversal, intersection, and evidence grounding---to reconstruct query-relevant context. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show strong performance, especially on multi-hop, temporal, and knowledge-update tasks. Ablations and a semantic-collapse probe support complementary contributions from epistemic separation, consolidation, and agentic retrieval. Code: https://github.com/Silent-Rain02/CogMem.

items.title: A Neuronally Active Bacterial Siderophore Manipulates Host Behavior and Longevity
items.abstract_or_text: Aging populations face a growing burden of neurodegenerative disease and behavioral decline. The microbiota is increasingly implicated in host physiology, highlighting an urgent need to understand how gut microbes modulate brain function and late life health. Here, we develop a high-throughput microbe-host screening platform to systematically dissect how bacterial genes shape organismal behavior. Using the Escherichia coli Keio library of 3,985 distinct non-essential single-gene deletion mutants in combination with Caenorhabditis elegans, we quantitatively profiled 768 behavioral features per bacterial clone and uncovered a coherent module of bacterial genes involved in iron homeostasis that robustly reprogrammed host behavior. Bacterial omics analyses revealed that alterations in iron homeostasis amplify siderophore production in a TCA cycle-dependent manner, and loss of enterobactin biosynthesis abolished the bacteria-induced changes in worm movement. Transcriptional, molecular and functional studies demonstrated that bacterial enterobactin activates host neuromuscular responses to shape both lifespan and healthspan in a manner dependent on the mitochondrial unfolded protein response. Thermal proteome profiling identified mitochondrial glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase and the electron-transfer flavoproteins A and B as enterobactin-binding targets that control mitochondrial function. Finally, genetic manipulation of neuronal mitochondrial and cytosolic reactive oxygen species via superoxide dismutase and catalase revealed that redox state modulates enterobactin-driven changes in movement and lifespan through the secretin-family GPCR neuropeptide receptor PDFR-1. Together, these findings establish microbial enterobactin as a non-canonical neurotransmitter regulating neuronal mitochondrial function, behavior and aging, defining a gut bacteria-brain axis with broad implications for maintaining late-life health.

items.title: A transferable perturbation proteomics framework for phenotype- 1 based annotation and antiproliferative potency scoring of antineoplastic agents
items.abstract_or_text: Although antineoplastic agents target diverse proteins, whether they converge on conserved cellular response states remains unclear. Here, we generate a TMTpro 18-plex quantitative proteomics atlas of 367 antineoplastic agents in HepG2 cells and identify recurrent drug response phenotypes (DRPs). The higher-order organization of DRP is conserved across seven independent proteomic datasets and shows limited concordance with chemical structure and annotated mechanisms of action. Projection of 189 external profiles representing 94 compounds achieves 42.7% balanced reference-DRP recovery, a 3.8-fold enrichment above the permutation-derived baseline. DRPs also encode antiproliferative potency, enabling derivation of a six-protein Composite Proteomic Score (CPS-6; TBL1X, NAPA, PLEKHA7, ACSL1, ARL8B, and CCDC90B) that retains associations with relative antiproliferative potency across independent proteomic and transcriptomic datasets. Proteomic similarity further reveals phenotypic convergence among mechanistically distinct compounds and enables mechanism annotation of external compounds and natural products. An interactive portal enables projection of new perturbation proteomes for phenotype-based annotation and antiproliferative potency estimation. Together, our study establishes a transferable proteomic framework for antineoplastic agents, providing a scalable resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation, drug repositioning, and phenotype-guided drug discovery.

items.title: Generative inverse design steers human hematopoietic cell fate in vitro
items.abstract_or_text: Inverse design has advanced the discovery of molecules and materials. Yet it remains largely unexplored for steering cell fate, where inputs are continuous, combinatorial culture conditions and outputs are distributions of cell states. Human hematopoiesis, in which combinations and doses of growth factors steer stem cells toward each blood lineage, is a demanding test case. While forward models can evaluate discrete conditions, the vast combinatorial space renders searching for a specific, target-producing design an intractable inverse problem. Here, we introduce LabCompass, an inverse-modeling framework that optimizes experimental designs toward candidates expected to produce specified target cell states, using a flow-matching generative model guided by cellular phenotypes predicted by a forward surrogate. We applied LabCompass to primary human CD34+ in vitro cultures, where continuous cytokine and small-molecule parameters govern hematopoietic cell fate. In a lab-in-the-loop setting, we experimentally validated model-driven designs and used these measurements to update the model across four successive loops. LabCompass recovered established lineage-inducing designs, improved predictions with new data, and enriched target populations across lineages. Incorporating new parameters expanded the design space and enriched rare populations beyond initial reach. Across loops, we generated a 78-million-cell spectral flow cytometry dataset and identified distinct culture conditions converging on the same target cell states. Our results establish generative inverse modeling as a compelling paradigm for navigating high-dimensional, continuous experimental spaces, and demonstrate that virtual cell models should be judged not only by how accurately they predict cellular responses, but also by how effectively they guide experiments toward desired biological outcomes.

items.title: Characterization of artificial riboswitches for Coxsackievirus B3 detection using machine learning
items.abstract_or_text: With the increase of recycled water to offset water demand, the potential possibility to spread contagious RNA viruses, such as Coxsackievirus B3, increases. However, detection of viral particles remains challenging because of low viral concentrations in wastewater and high mutation rates of the RNA virus. Robust monitoring is needed with low cost and low infrastructure technologies to increase accessibility of monitoring technologies worldwide. Novel viral detection methods have been developed, based on synthetic riboswitches that bind to the target virus and trigger a reporter gene, thus amplifying the detection signals. Such monitoring technologies can leverage machine learning to optimize the candidate nucleic acid sequences used for detection. To support the design of effective riboswitches, we present a machine learning model for classifying riboswitch performance, integrating RNA sequence data with secondary structural features based on free energy calculations and parameters that represent single strandedness. This model uses a sparsely gated Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to route sequence and thermodynamic features to specialized experts, achieving strong generalization performance across cross-validation and held-out testing. When evaluated against baseline Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gaussian Naive Bayes, and Dense Neural Network classifiers, the MoE model demonstrated near-zero classification errors. Furthermore, post-hoc feature importance and k-mer analyzes reveal that near-perfect predictive performance in silico is strongly driven by sequence constructs in addition to generalizable folding mechanics. An ablation study of numerical feature and sequence inputs showed that while the Dense Neural Network also achieved high accuracy across all ablation conditions, the MoE architecture was retained as the primary model because its specialized subnetworks do not require all model parameters to be activated offering a potential computational advantage.

items.title: From Static Material Design to Predictive Open-Loop Control via Chemistry–Architecture Coupling in a Moving-Boundary Reaction–Diffusion Framework
Multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential for the energetics and finite temperature structure of Pt surfaces and nanoparticles
items.abstract_or_text: Accurate accounting of exposed facets and surface sites is central to understanding metal nanoparticle catalysts, but modelling their structure at finite temperatures is computationally expensive. We benchmark the universal interatomic potential UMA (Universal Model for Atoms, Open Catalyst 2020 task) against Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional theory (PBE-DFT) for Pt. UMA underestimates the surface energies of all 13 facets by 11-17 % and the excess energies of 28 differently shaped nanoparticles, each containing less than 500 atoms, most strongly for small particles. We distill UMA into a compact Deep Potential model by pre-training on UMA labelled bulk and slab data, then fine-tune it on a small PBE-DFT dataset that includes nanoparticles. The resulting multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential (MF-MLIP) gives a surface-energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 2.8 meV Å−2, 21 % lower than a DFT only model trained on the same data. On six nanoparticles, the MF-MLIP improves force accuracy over UMA, reducing the force RMSE by 29-52 %, with the largest gains at surface, edge and vertex atoms. Molecular dynamics at 500 K shows Pt(111) retaining its termination while Pt(100) and Pt(110) change strongly. At 500-700 K, the nanoparticles lose vertex sites and gain edge sites, and some restructure away from their ideal shapes. On the same CPU hardware, the MF-MLIP runs molecular dynamics simulations 60-100 times faster than UMA.

items.title: Batch Before You Lift: Scalable Topological Deep Learning on Large Graphs
items.abstract_or_text: Topological Deep Learning extends graph-based learning to higher-order domains, such as hypergraphs, cellular, and simplicial complexes. These domains are typically constructed from patterns in an input graph through a process of graph lifting. Full-domain training constructs and stores the complete lifted representation before model execution. On large and dense datasets like Reddit (233k nodes and 57.3M edges), this global materialization becomes a severe computational bottleneck, often rendering training infeasible. To address this limitation, we introduce Cluster-TNN, a domain-agnostic framework that avoids this bottleneck by lifting locally instead. After partitioning the input graph during preprocessing, at runtime Cluster-TNN dynamically samples groups of node clusters, reconstructs their induced subgraphs to form mini-batches, and applies the chosen lifting within each mini-batch. Retaining all edges among sampled nodes preserves the connectivity needed to construct higher-order structures across clusters, producing topological mini-batches that existing Topological Neural Networks can process directly. Across 21 matched comparisons with full-graph execution, Cluster-TNN reduces peak GPU memory in every configuration, by 83.2% on average while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Notably, such a reduction enables, to our knowledge, the first training of multiple different higher-order Topological Neural Networks on large datasets such as Reddit and OGBN Products. These results establish Cluster-TNN as a general strategy for scaling Topological Deep Learning beyond the limitations of global domain construction.

items.title: A structure-preserving neural density functional for the ions of a polymer electrolyte
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting the structure and response of inhomogeneous polymer electrolytes requires a description of ion correlations that retains molecular-scale accuracy while remaining transferable across spatial scales and geometries. We develop a neural density functional for electrolytes that preserves spatial symmetries, thermodynamic integrability and the Noether identities, with perfect screening recovered in stable, noncritical bulk states. Its nonlinear density dependence captures the concentration-dependent correlations missed by a pair closure, including a crossover from enhanced to suppressed long-wavelength number fluctuations at strong coupling. The functional describes density profiles at an untrained salt concentration and predicts bulk structure factors and the long-wavelength number response. Trained solely on planar density and internal-force profiles from molecular dynamics, the functional predicts ionic structure in larger domains and in two-dimensional external fields. On the same ion data, it is more accurate than three other neural density-functional architectures and keeps its accuracy with a quarter of the training runs, where the errors of the best alternative grow by about two thirds. The spatial transferability provides a necessary foundation for connecting molecular correlations to continuum predictions at larger scales.

items.title: Safe Actions Alone Do Not Ensure Safe Agents: Identifying Unfulfilled Obligations with Guard Models
items.abstract_or_text: Guard models are increasingly used to safeguard LLM-based agents, primarily by identifying actions that agents are forbidden to perform. However, identifying forbidden actions alone is insufficient to ensure agent safety. In this paper, we argue that agent safety also depends on identifying required yet unperformed safety-critical actions, which we call obligations. Our preliminary study on a popular benchmark for evaluating safety shows that 56.92% of GLM-5.3 trajectories contain unfulfilled obligations, compared with only 30.00% containing forbidden actions. This finding reveals unfulfilled obligations as a major and previously overlooked source of safety risk. However, to our knowledge, no existing benchmark evaluates whether guard models can identify these obligations. To close this gap, we introduce ObligationBench, the first benchmark for evaluating the capability of obligation identification, comprising 240 expert-validated trajectories covering issue resolution, feature development, and terminal operations. Our evaluation of 14 representative models reveals substantial limitations: the highest recall and exact-match rate are only 48.97% and 10.00%, respectively. To address these limitations, we develop ObligationGuard using 40,000 synthetic training examples. ObligationGuard achieves 57.52% recall and an exact-match rate of 21.67%, surpassing all evaluated models on both metrics. We call on the community to incorporate obligation identification into the design and evaluation of future guard models to improve agent safety.

items.title: Constitutional Gating and Deterministic Recovery for Multi-Agent LLM Negotiation: Ablations Against a Stateful Adversarial Gatekeeper
items.abstract_or_text: Multi-agent LLM systems negotiating with a stateful counterpart waste model calls in three ways: polite loops that never meet the counterpart's hidden acceptance condition, malformed outputs that trigger retries, and compliance deadlocks in which the counterpart demands something the agent must refuse. We study a three-part control stack - a 5-Pillar runtime constitution, a 4-tier swarm (Director, three-agent majority vote, Monitor, schema hard gate) and Cognitive Annealing (deterministic deadlock detection, atomic purge of the agent-side context, a canonical recovery message) - against a released adversarial Gatekeeper whose acceptance rules are fixed regular expressions and whose LLM only renders reply text. The testbed has a known solution: it measures whether the stack executes a constitution-aligned strategy against swarm drift and recovers from deadlock, not whether it discovers anything. In five runs per configuration (30 runs; Gemini 2.5 Pro agents, Claude Haiku 4.5 Gatekeeper) we find: (i) the constitution and Director make an acceptable framing possible but not reliable - 0/5 baseline unlocks versus 1/5 and 2/5 with the constitution; when the swarm unlocks it does so in one turn with 7-8 calls and about 15k tokens (67-73% below baseline); when it does not, it costs 17-38% more; (ii) the Monitor and hard gate do not reduce unlocks and leave an audit trail; (iii) under a honeytrap-to-compliance deadlock, LLM-only steering escapes 0 of 5 times while atomic purge plus a canonical strike escapes 5 of 5 (Fisher p = 0.008) at the same call budget, with zero calls for the strike. LLM-written strikes failed the deterministic pre-flight 5 of 5 times although an LLM Monitor had approved four. Pre-registered hypotheses on average call and token reduction were not supported. Cost is bounded in every arm by deterministic stop rules; the stack adds recovery at no extra model cost.

items.title: When to Intervene? State-Aware Sparse Manipulation in Federated Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Federated reinforcement learning (FRL) enables distributed agents to collaboratively train decision-making policies, but its decentralized training process also exposes global policy learning to Byzantine manipulation. Existing poisoning attacks primarily focus on how to construct malicious updates, while trajectory-level intervention timing remains largely implicit. In sequential decision making, however, where an intervention is applied can alter subsequent trajectories and learning signals. Through controlled experiments, we find that changing the selected trajectory states materially alters attack efficacy even when the malicious-update construction is fixed. We therefore identify when as a distinct attack dimension and introduce the Viability-constrained Behavioral Steering Attack (V-BSA), which uses local policy uncertainty to select sparse intervention states and applies envelope-constrained behavioral steering. Across discrete-action benchmarks, V-BSA achieves substantial degradation against robust aggregators and ensemble defenses with only a fraction of the interventions used by dense poisoning, while revealing task- and aggregation-dependent boundaries. Overall, our results highlight intervention timing as a distinct dimension of sequential robustness in FRL. The code is available at https://github.com/Yodeesy/V-BSA

items.title: NOMOS: Compiling Written Policies into Statically Verified Tool-Call Gates for LLM Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Tool-using LLM agents violate the policies they are deployed to enforce, often silently. Prior defenses hand-write rules, query an LLM verifier per action, or compile policies through heavyweight formal machinery. Naive compilation fails: extracted rules block the tool satisfying their own precondition, or read arguments their tool lacks. NOMOS, a four-pass compiler, turns a natural-language policy into a deterministic tool-call gate; static verification with tool-schema-level checks alone (no prover, solver, or LLM) repairs or rejects 37% (airline) and 13% (retail) of candidates, without which most shipped rules are inoperable. Replaying compiled rules over undefended transcripts flags bindings that refuse legitimate work (a development binding refused 95.9% of task-passing calls); no evaluation binding is flagged. On τ^2-bench the gate cuts violations of reference-encoded clauses among state-changing calls from 66.3% to 2.6% (airline) and 30.8% to 6.9% (retail), raising airline task success significantly for 2 \le k \le 4; a 26B on-premise compilation is not significantly worse than hand-written or frontier-compiled rules. Unlike AgentDojo's shipped defenses, it reaches a zero attack success rate (ASR) on banking, where nine attack families collapse onto three structural rules. On the other three suites its ASR is at most 3.6%, from goals with no tool call to govern and one write admitted by a binding weaker than its clause; a second agent model, Llama-3.3-70B, reproduces the effect on both benchmarks. Decisions take microseconds without an LLM call, at a domain-dependent benign-utility cost; compilation runs on-premise on open-weight gemma-4-26B.

items.title: Validated Semantic Scoring Improves Filtering of Generic Concepts from Knowledge-Graphs for Drug Repurposing Queries
items.abstract_or_text: When an ontology-based biomedical knowledge graph (a KG, containing information about genes, pathways, phenotypes, and molecular interactions) is analyzed using a computational reasoning system, the system can return unwanted generic concepts. Such generic concepts, in the context of a query about potential drug treatments for a disease, might include 'pharmaceutical preparations' or 'antibiotics'. Answers can be filtered based on hand-curated block-lists or ontology Information Content (IC), but to our knowledge, (1) neither filtering method has been validated against expert judgments of generality, and (2) IC is not available for the majority of nodes in the representative KG used in this work. In this study, three domain experts rated representative lists of KG concepts for generality. We built a semantic precision score (SPS) from a concept's name and description alone, using a biomedical language model (BioLORD). For the purpose of filtering generic answers from biomedical query results, we compared (using queries for 200 diseases) the SPS against a curated concept block-list and two IC thresholds. IC agreed moderately with the experts (Spearman's {rho} = 0.59), but correlations were negligible or negative within IC bands. The SPS was well-correlated with the experts ({rho} = 0.76) globally and within SPS bands, and remained informative on concepts without IC ({rho} = 0.59). Hard filtering of query results using the SPS removed 1,502 of 33,161 query answers, nearly three times the block-list's 513, while removing fewer of the query-specific DrugCentral indications. Hard filtering by IC removed either few answers or many approved drugs. We additionally compared the filtering methods' performance on an independent evaluation set of queries for 200 diseases. The SPS filter removed 5,135 of 91,203 answers compared with the block-list's 1,419 and lost none of 1,296 indications compared with 17. Further, SPS filtering removed approved drugs no more often from the half of DrugCentral not used in training than from the half used in training. Semantic meaning captures expert judgments of specificity more faithfully than ontology position, and semantic scoring can replace IC and manually maintained block-lists for filtering drug-repurposing results.

items.title: Dynamic Modulation of Neural Cell Identity Maintenance via Lysine Acetyltransferase Type 3 Protein Targeted Degradation
items.abstract_or_text: Cell identity acquisition during central nervous system development leads to the establishment of cell-specific transcriptional programs. Once acquired, this identity must be actively maintained, among other molecular mechanisms, by the acetylation of cell-type-specific regulatory regions carried out by the lysine acetyltransferases type 3 (KAT3) proteins CBP and p300. Here, we characterize the rapid transcriptional and physiological consequences of KAT3 elimination in neuronal and glial lineages by means of a KAT3-specific PROTAC degrader, providing strong evidence for their central role as neural identity wardens. Importantly, the restoration of KAT3 proteins in glial cells after cell identity erasure resulted in the recovery of the original transcriptome and physiological functions, probing the dynamic nature of neural cell identities. These findings expand the role of CBP/p300 as identity wardens and challenge our perception of terminal cellular identities as static irrevocable states, opening new avenues for neural identity manipulation with biomedical purposes.
